target: Archebodd hi ddau gwpanaid o de a sgon.
english: She ordered two cups of tea and a scone.
tip: The number ‘dau’ (two) soft-mutates the next noun: ‘cwpanaid’ becomes ‘gwpanaid’. ‘ddau gwpanaid o de’ = two cups of tea.

target: Wyt ti'n hoffi coffi neu de yn y bore?
english: Do you like coffee or tea in the morning?
tip: ‘wyt ti'n’ starts an informal yes/no question. ‘wyt ti'n hoffi’ means do you like.

target: Rhedodd e'r ras mewn tair awr a deg munud.
english: He ran the race in three hours and ten minutes.
tip: ‘mewn’ means in before an indefinite noun: ‘mewn tair awr’ = in three hours. Use ‘yn’ before a definite noun.

target: Cafodd yr hen gar teuluol ei werthu'r wythnos diwethaf oherwydd bod angen un mwy ar gyfer y plant.
english: The old family car was sold last week because they needed a bigger one for the children.
tip: The passive uses ‘cael’ plus a possessive: ‘ei werthu’, literally its selling. ‘cafodd ... ei werthu’ = it was sold.
‘dw i'n’, ‘rwy'n’ and ‘rydw i'n’ all mean I am. ‘dw i'n’ is the casual spoken form, as in ‘dw i'n llwglyd’.
‘ei’ meaning it or him softens the next word: ‘cymryd’ becomes ‘gymryd’ in ‘ei gymryd’.
The word ‘â’ triggers aspirate mutation on c, p, t: ‘Conwy’ becomes ‘Chonwy’ in ‘ymweld â Chonwy’.
‘fy’ (my) triggers nasal mutation: ‘cydweithwyr’ becomes ‘nghydweithwyr’ in ‘fy nghydweithwyr’.
‘pump’ (five) drops to ‘pum’ before a noun. ‘astudio pum pwnc’ means study five subjects.
The article shortens to ‘'r’ after a vowel: ‘hoffi’ plus ‘y’ becomes ‘hoffi'r’ in ‘hoffi'r farchnad’.

target: Caria 'mlaen i siarad Cymraeg, rwyt ti'n gwella.
english: Carry on speaking Welsh, you're improving.
tip: ‘rwyt ti'n’ means you are, informal singular. ‘rwyt ti'n gwella’ means you are improving.

target: Coginiáis i swper i'r teulu i gyd.
english: I cooked dinner for the whole family.
tip: The ending ‘-ais’ marks a completed past I-action. ‘coginiáis i’ means I cooked.

target: Mae gen i ddau frawd a thair chwaer.
english: I have two brothers and three sisters.
tip: In north Wales possession uses ‘gan’. ‘mae gen i’ means I have, as in ‘mae gen i ddau frawd’.

target: Mae'n bwysig gwybod pryd i ddefnyddio 'chi'.
english: It's important to know when to use 'chi'.
tip: ‘pryd’ means when in questions and indirect clauses. ‘pryd i ddefnyddio’ means when to use.

target: Dw i wedi colli'r trên, pryd mae'r un nesaf?
english: I've missed the train, when is the next one?
tip: ‘wedi’ plus a verb-noun makes the perfect: ‘dw i wedi colli’ means I have missed.

target: Dw i'n mynd ar y fferi o Gaergybi i Ddulyn.
english: I'm going on the ferry from Holyhead to Dublin.
tip: ‘i’ (to) triggers soft mutation: ‘Dulyn’ becomes ‘Ddulyn’ in ‘i Ddulyn’.
To form an adverb, put ‘yn’ before an adjective and it soft-mutates: ‘da’ becomes ‘dda’. ‘dawnsio'n dda’ = dances well.
‘yn’ before a verb-noun marks an ongoing action: ‘mae e'n gweithio’ = he is working, literally he is at working.
Adjectives usually soft-mutate after a feminine noun: ‘dewr’ becomes ‘ddewr’ in ‘ferch ddewr’ = brave girl.
Feminine nouns normally soft-mutate after the (‘y’, ‘yr’, ‘'r’): ‘canolfan’ becomes ‘ganolfan’, as in ‘mae'r ganolfan’ = the centre.
‘bron â’ means almost, and ‘â’ aspirate-mutates the next verb: ‘cyrraedd’ becomes ‘chyrraedd’.
The word ‘o’ (of) soft-mutates the next noun: ‘cymeriad’ becomes ‘gymeriad’. ‘dipyn o gymeriad’ = quite a character.
Yes/no questions open with the verb form: ‘ydych chi'n gwerthu ...?’ = do you sell ...?
Comparatives usually add ‘-ach’ and take ‘na’ for than: ‘tlws’ becomes ‘tlysach’. ‘dlysach na'r llun’ = prettier than the picture.
‘pa’ (which) soft-mutates the following noun: ‘diwrnod’ becomes ‘ddiwrnod’. ‘pa ddiwrnod’ = what day.
Past-tense I-verbs usually end in ‘-ais’, and the ‘i’ pronoun follows: ‘ddwedais i’ means I said.

target: Mae gwyliau celfyddydol ym mhob man.
tip: ‘yn’ becomes ‘ym’ and nasal-mutates the next word: ‘pob’ becomes ‘mhob’. ‘ym mhob man’ = everywhere.

target: Dych chi'n adnabod y dyn yna?
tip: Welsh splits know: ‘adnabod’ for people, ‘gwybod’ for facts. ‘adnabod y dyn’ = know the man.

target: Ffoniais i fy chwaer o'r orsaf.
english: I called my sister from the station.
tip: Soft mutation can delete ‘g’ entirely: ‘gorsaf’ becomes ‘orsaf’ after ‘o'r’, giving ‘o'r orsaf’ (from the station).

target: Mae hi'n bwrw hen wragedd a ffyn.
tip: ‘hen’ (old) comes before its noun and soft-mutates it: ‘gwragedd’ becomes ‘wragedd’ in ‘hen wragedd’ = old women.
